fields: Autonomous driving systems at SAE J3016 Level 4 or higher cannot presuppose driver intervention; when a fault occurs, they must therefore execute a minimal risk maneuver (MRM) that brings the vehicle to a minimal risk condition (MRC) on its own. ISO 26262 requires that detection and response be completed within the Fault Tolerant Time Interval (FTTI), the time allowed from fault occurrence to a hazardous event, while SOTIF (ISO 21448) requires the management of hazards arising from sensor performance limitations.

The open-source autonomous driving stack Autoware provides comfortable_stop and emergency_stop as its default MRMs. However, in the version and execution configuration evaluated in this study (Autoware 0.39.0, Chapter 4, Section 1), most of the injected sensor faults were not detected by the stack's own diagnostics, and the available fallbacks were limited to in-lane stop-type MRMs. Above all, no supervisory layer is provided that "evaluates the type and degree of a sensor fault together with the remaining maneuvering capability, selects between evacuation and stopping accordingly, and further limits the speed of the evacuation movement to match the fault state." The contribution of this study lies in this supervisory layer, not in the shoulder maneuver itself. We state explicitly that this observation is not a claim about Autoware in general, but a fact limited to the evaluated version and execution configuration.

An in-lane stop is simple to implement and immediate, but a stopped vehicle blocks following traffic and creates opportunities for secondary collisions, and this cost persists until the lane occupancy is cleared. Conversely, continuing to drive without detecting the fault extends the distance over which the vehicle is exposed to hazards under degraded perception — in the unmonitored observations of this study, in single-run-per-type unmonitored observations the stock stack effectively completed 238–275 m of the route with faults injected (Chapter 5, Section 2). The design space of fault response thus has three axes: "whether to stop now, how far to move, and, if moving, how fast to move."

When a human driver senses something wrong with the vehicle, the priority is to pull over to the shoulder as far as circumstances permit. Automating this shoulder-evacuation-type MRM requires three prior judgments (Figure 1-1): (i) distinguishing whether the fault is "mild enough to allow moving to the shoulder" or "severe enough to require stopping immediately"; (ii) a continuous evaluation of the type and degree of the fault that makes this distinction possible (a binary normal/faulty diagnostic state is insufficient); and (iii) managing the risk of movement itself in a degraded state when movement is chosen — the stopping distance in a dart-out situation. This study implements these, respectively, as a continuous health score, risk- and remaining-capability-based state transitions, and a conservative remaining-capability-based speed cap (fixed at 3.0 m/s).

Finally, simulation-based safety claims stand only on the reliability of the collision determination itself. In the course of the experiments, this study empirically uncovered cases in which the simulator's collision sensor configuration remained silent; prompted by this, we built a dual determination scheme consisting of a real-time ledger of the ego vehicle's collision sensor and a pedestrian physics oracle, and used it as the basis for the safety conclusions (Chapter 4, Section 5).

The proposed supervisory layer is an add-on layer that does not replace the stack itself. Monitoring operates solely by subscribing to sensor topics, intervention occurs only through standard interfaces, and the execution of stopping maneuvers is delegated to the stock stack. This non-intrusive design leaves the certification boundary of the base stack undisturbed while allowing defects in the decision layer and the execution layer to be traced separately at the log level (Chapter 3, Section 8). At the same time, it carries the limitation that execution quality is dependent on the base stack — this trade-off is discussed in Chapter 6.

RQ1. If sensor faults are estimated as a continuous health score, can the response strategy (shoulder/parking-lot evacuation vs. immediate stop deferral) be selected differentially according to the type and degree of the fault? How much does that selection reduce exposure to the fault state?

RQ2. What does a shoulder-evacuation-type MRM gain and lose compared with a stop-type MRM? What temporal structure does the trade-off between immediate collision risk and lane clearance / final safe position have?

RQ3. How does conservative low-speed movement based on remaining capability (a fixed speed cap) change safety at the level of dart-out encounters, and what does its limiting condition — the transient before deceleration is complete — imply?

First, we propose a behavior-tree-based sensor monitoring module. For each sensor, it independently scores data freshness (timeout), data quality (noise and valid ratio), and physical consistency (residuals and bias), and composes these across eight-direction spatial sectors and functional capability (perception and localization) layers, publishing the result as a continuous health score.

Second, we propose a risk- and remaining-capability-based MRM supervisor. According to health-score bands, it selects between shoulder/parking-lot evacuation (MRM_MOVE) and deferral to the stock stopping behavior (MRM_DEFER); the evacuation site is chosen by a cost function reflecting degraded-state exposure time, traffic-light observability, and sector deficits; and during evacuation movement, a conservative fixed speed cap (3.0 m/s; below the model-derived upper bound (under nominal parameters) v_max≈3.89 m/s), back-computed from the stopping distance model d=vτ+v²/2a, is imposed on the planning layer. The effect of the cap is verified at the causal level in a dose-response experiment restricted to settled encounters where the cap actually held (Chapter 5, Section 6).

Third, we establish a dual scheme for simulation collision determination as a methodology. It combines a real-time ledger of the ego collision sensor (RAW-HIT) with a pedestrian physics oracle (kinematic anomalies at collision), and identifies the determination pitfalls inherent in the experiment runner's termination labels and the official infraction records.

Fourth, as a validation contribution, we perform encounter-level quantitative validation and large-scale matrix validation. Using a pedestrian dart-out distance ladder, we empirically measure the avoidance/collision boundary by speed (8–11 m at 4.2 m/s, 7–8 m at 3.0 m/s) and compare it against the stopping distance model; through transient-versus-settled encounter observations, we show that the residual risk of evacuation is concentrated in the post-detection transient — a quantitative observation supporting the need to shorten detection and response times (widening the margin within the FTTI); and with a single closed-loop experimental framework totaling 1,862 valid cases — the fault type × severity × traffic density × method campaigns plus the dose-response encounter experiment — we quantify the monitoring and evacuation behavior, the reduction in exposure, and the causal effect of the cap.

The novelty of this study lies not in the individual techniques (CUSUM, residual monitoring, noisy-OR fusion, the stopping distance model, and so on — each is a known technique), but in the system architecture that integrates them into a continuous health score and combines it with remaining maneuvering capability, risk deferral, and movement speed limiting to select MRMs in a graded manner, and in the encounter-level closed-loop demonstration whose determination reliability is secured at the methodological level.

Chapter 2 reviews the relevant standards and prior research, and Chapter 3 describes the architecture of the proposed system and each of its components. Chapter 4 presents the experimental environment, the fault model, the collision determination methodology, and the encounter experiment design; Chapter 5 presents the results; Chapter 6 presents the limitations and discussion; and Chapter 7 concludes.

Related work is organized into six strands (Sections 1-6): standards and regulation, time budgets, detection theory and degradation models, fallback and MRM planning, capability-based self-monitoring, and simulation-based evaluation and fault injection; Section 7 compares them with this study.

The foundational frameworks of functional safety, SOTIF, and driving-automation level taxonomy [1-3], together with production-regulation and safety-case standards [4-7], consistently require runtime monitoring and responses to degradation. ISO 23793-1:2024 [51], which addresses MRM directly, specifies a classification framework for MRM types and the principle of "selecting the type according to the situation," but covers only the simplest types (straight-line and in-lane stops); shoulder stops are being standardized as Part 2.

As a reference from an adjacent domain, the industrial driverless truck standard ISO 3691-4 [60], rather than prohibiting movement in a degraded state outright, prescribes the principle of "limited speed for limited capability," combining monitored speed limits with stop functions; the conservative low-speed MRM movement of this study (Chapter 3, Section 6) transfers this principle to autonomous-driving MRM. However, these standards do not provide a method for continuously estimating the kind and degree of a fault and selecting the response and speed accordingly.
2. FTTI and the Derivation of Time Budgets

ISO 26262 (2nd edition) defines the FTTI as "the minimum time from the occurrence of a fault to the point at which a hazardous event may occur, assuming the safety mechanisms are not activated," but provides no concrete values; the FTTI must be derived per safety goal from vehicle dynamics and scenarios — Bosch's estimation method [8] is a representative case, deriving 1.4–1.8 s in a lane-keeping-loss scenario. As risk metrics, time-to-collision (TTC) [9] and its extensions [10], and RSS [11], which formalizes safe distances with worst-case kinematics, are standard. This study implements this framework as a dynamic detection budget that ties the detection-time requirement to driving risk (including the FDTI/FRTI and safety-margin decomposition framework, Chapter 3, Section 4), and, by measuring at the encounter level that the residual risk of evacuation-type MRMs concentrates in the post-detection transient (Chapter 5, Sections 5-6), provides an observation supporting the need to shorten detection and response times (widening the margin within the FTTI).
3. Fault Detection Theory and Sensor Degradation Models

Classical FDI has developed along two lines: residual generation and decision [12-15] and sequential change detection [16][17]; the lidar quality channel of this study borrows the CUSUM [16] from the latter (Chapter 3, Section 2). These theories cover only up to "detection"; the selection of maneuvers after detection is outside their scope.
B. Empirical Evidence and Models of Lidar Degradation

Lidar degradation is covered by fault taxonomies [57], field measurements and physical models of soiling and rainfall [53-56], and adverse-weather simulation and quantification studies [20-23][58][59]. The sparsification (lidar soiling occlusion, lso) model of this study follows field measurements of soiling-induced detection-range reduction [55], and the clutter (lidar clutter, lcl) model follows the attenuation, jitter, and threshold formulas for rain scattering [53] and near-range-biased clutter [54] (Chapter 4, Section 2). Autoware preprocessing and diagnostics [18] and PCL [19] aim at the "removal" of outliers, a purpose distinct from continuous "scoring" of sensor condition.

The camera failure-mode taxonomy [24] is the reference for the cn and cf injections of this study; for the IMU, the separate evaluation of measurement white noise and time-accumulating bias [25][26] serves as the reference, and for GNSS, the failure-mode framework [62], urban error measurements [27], and integrity monitoring [28][29]; the multipath-type correlated bias (gm) is injected following a first-order Gauss-Markov model [61].

Among safe-stop planning approaches for faults and performance limits, the trajectory-planning line [30-32] addresses the parallel maintenance of stop trajectories, optimal-control formulations, and online verification, but takes the assessment of the fault and the choice of response as given. In the fallback-strategy line, Emzivat et al. [33] proposed, as a fallback for systems with impaired monitoring capability, virtual obstacles and TTC-based deceleration, and Reschka and Maurer [34] pointed out that the "safe state" of an automated vehicle is situation-dependent and that an in-lane stop is not always safe — the same concern from which this study starts.

The closest prior work is the line of sensor-fault-presupposing evacuation and adaptive MRM. Xue et al. [49][50], presupposing a forward-sensor fault, proposed a safe-zone stop fallback under MPC safety constraints and an adaptive MPC extension based on virtual vehicles in unobserved regions; Tang et al. [48] proposed a method that, under multiple sensor faults, adaptively selects MRM behaviors (deceleration, lane-keeping stop, shoulder-oriented stop, etc.) using HAZOP risk analysis and virtual-object, TTC, and THW evaluation, and validated it in a MATLAB-CARLA closed loop. The differences from this study are as follows. (i) They presuppose that the sensor-fault state is given and address the subsequent maneuvers and selection, whereas this study starts from estimating the occurrence, kind, and severity of the fault through online monitoring of sensor data. (ii) As selection criteria they use TTC/THW with surrounding traffic, whereas this study combines, in addition to risk grace time, the remaining perception and localization capability, and further limits the speed of the evacuation movement itself to match the fault state. (iii) The focus of validation differs: rather than checking whether maneuvers succeed in representative scenarios, this study performed closed-loop behavioral verification of 1,862 valid cases on a real open-source stack (Autoware), together with pedestrian-encounter experiments whose verdict reliability was secured at the methodology level.

The open-source stack Autoware [18] provides stop-type MRMs and shoulder pull-over search (goal_planner), but the version and configuration evaluated (Chapter 4, Section 1) had no supervisory layer that differentially triggers responses and limits speed based on health score and remaining capability — that layer is the contribution of this study.

The skill and ability graphs of Reschka et al. [35] and their development-process extension [36] form a lineage that models functional capabilities as hierarchical graphs for use in online monitoring and decision making; the sector-capability composition of this study (Chapter 3, Section 3) is an implementation that couples capability scores directly to MRM level selection and the movement speed cap. Runtime monitor case studies [37], SMOF [38], and verification challenges [39] are adjacent lines, and behavior trees [40][41] are used as the parallel-composition and execution-tracing structure of the monitoring node based on BehaviorTree.CPP [42] (implementation structure — Chapter 3, Section 1).

CARLA [43] is the standard platform for fault-injection research, and stack-targeted fault-injection evaluations — DriveFI [44], resilience evaluation [45], AV-FUZZER [46], and the scenario language Scenic [47] — are studies that "inject faults to find vulnerabilities," the opposite direction from this study, which has the stack itself detect and grade the injected faults and select a response (this study uses the same injection techniques as a means of verification). The experimental infrastructure of this study is built on AWCL [52], the Autoware-CARLA-coupled leaderboard framework (released by the Institute of Automotive Technology at TUM), as a fully automated harness that restarts the simulator for every case (Chapter 4). Furthermore, no report was found that addresses the reliability of simulated collision verdicts — collision-sensor silence, termination-label misclassification — at the methodology level; this study treats it in a formal section (Chapter 4, Section 5).

The proposed system consists of two independent nodes (Figure 3-1). The monitoring module cdr_monitor inspects each sensor at 10 Hz on a behavior-tree basis (the behavior tree is not an algorithmic contribution but an implementation structure for parallel composition, module replacement, and execution tracing), computing and publishing a per-sensor health score (0–1); the detectors comprise three families: timeout (freshness), quality (noise, valid ratio), and physics (residual, bias). The supervisor mrm_supervisor subscribes to the scores and operates a state machine: for evacuation it changes the route via the Autoware AD API and imposes a speed cap on the planning layer, and for deferral it triggers the stop of the stock mrm_handler through the diagnostic graph. Execution of the stopping maneuver is handled by goal_planner and mrm_handler, and modification of the main stack is minimized by injecting monitoring units into the diagnostic graph.

The reception and evaluation cycles are separated: reception accumulates at each sensor's native rate (LiDAR 20 Hz, IMU 100 Hz, etc.), while evaluation runs at 10 Hz (delay contributed by the evaluation cycle ≤0.1 s). The 100 ms evaluation cycle is consistent with the periodic supervision structure of the AUTOSAR Watchdog Manager [7] and also matches the decision cycle of the Autoware planning layer.

The supervisor switches its response using dual thresholds on the health score (upper 0.7, lower 0.3) (Figure 3-3): from NORMAL, falling below the upper threshold triggers evacuation movement (MRM_MOVE); completion of evacuation triggers evacuation parking (MRM_PARKED); and falling to or below the lower threshold, or a collapse of localization confidence, triggers deferral to the stock stop (MRM_DEFER). As safeguards against false activation, it employs a post-boot health check, a route-change non-response watchdog, a candidate-stagnation blacklist, and a creep guard. The selection is not frozen while moving, either — if a rear vehicle keeps occupying the approach during a parking approach or maneuver (within 10 m for 20 s), the parking-lot candidates that require reversing are penalized and re-selection demotes the target to a shoulder stop; movement stalls and route-change non-responses get a bounded number of retries; and candidate exhaustion or a health collapse en route falls back to DEFER (en-route re-evaluation — Figure 3-1).

The dual thresholds (upper 0.7, lower 0.3) distinguish NORMAL, DEGRADED, and CRITICAL; ● denotes selection according to the cost ordering, ○ a fallback upon movement failure, and × non-selection. A dead sensor goes directly to the degraded stage regardless of the thresholds, and if no reachable candidate exists, the state is demoted to the critical stage and deferred to the stock stop.

The dual thresholds serve both chattering prevention and grade separation; since the decay constants were designed so that a wide insensitive gap lies between the score under fault and the normal score, the behavior is determined by the three-band structure (normal/evacuation/deferral) rather than by the precise placement of the thresholds.

The timing rules for state transitions are split in two according to the nature of the evidence. Degradation-type (noise) faults are statistical evidence and therefore require sustained confirmation: 1.0 s for band entry; 2.0 s at the floor (≤0.3), because deferral is an irreversible terminal decision; and a 5.0 s recovery grace period when, within the band, localization confidence falls short of the movement minimum (0.5) — this prevents the misjudgment of making a terminal decision on an instantaneous value that dips deeper than the settled value immediately after fault onset (measured 0.44 versus settled 0.58), and in a sensitivity check, varying the grace period over 0.5–5.0 s left the results unchanged (gn-mid, 10 repetitions per condition). In contrast, for hard fails (signal loss — confirmed death past the 850 ms freshness deadline), the persistence of silence is itself already accumulated evidence, so the above confirmations are not redundantly applied: once death is confirmed and at least one live sensor remains (simultaneous silence of all sensors is identified and excluded as a simulation frame-freeze artifact), the band confirmation is skipped, and under visibility/candidate conditions where recovery is impossible, deferral is immediate with no grace period or retry. Route costs of evacuation-site candidates are periodically precomputed during normal driving (cycling one candidate every 2 ticks), eliminating selection latency at decision time. As a result, detection and adjudication of hard fails complete within the 1.5 s deadline (measured in Chapter 5, Section 7).

The evacuation candidate layer (shoulders and parking lots) was built by manual annotation of road_shoulder/parking_lot subtypes on the lanelet2 map, with the criteria of a minimum shoulder length sufficient to complete the stopping maneuver, mainline connectivity, and consistency between the entry polygon and the goal point. Shoulder candidates are lanelets sharing a boundary line with the mainline and are connected to the route graph; parking-lot candidates are closed polygonal areas. Manual annotation limits the verification scope to the annotated segments (limitations and automatic-extraction alternatives are discussed in Chapter 6).
8. Boundary and Interface with the Execution Layer

The system's scope of responsibility is detection, decision, candidate selection, and the speed cap ("whether to evacuate, where, when, and how fast"), while execution of the stopping maneuver is delegated to Autoware. In MRM_MOVE, the evacuation goal is delivered via AD API route resetting, and mission_planner's replanning and goal_planner's pull-over maneuver execute it — the shoulder-entry maneuver itself is a stock goal_planner capability and was not modified in this work. In MRM_DEFER, ERROR is injected into the diagnostic graph to trigger the stop of the stock mrm_handler (a boundary established to separate decision from execution).

The experimental stage is a closed-loop environment coupling the CARLA 0.9.16 simulator with Autoware 0.39.0 (Figure 4-1). The integration infrastructure is based on AWCL [52], the Autoware-CARLA leaderboard framework released by the Institute of Automotive Technology at TUM (C++ bridge, vehicle digital twin, scenario runner); CARLA runs on the host, while the bridge, leaderboard, and Autoware run in independent containers. The map is a custom vector map of CARLA Town07 (a low-speed urban/rural mix) annotated with shoulder and parking-lot candidates, the speed limit is 15 km/h (4.2 m/s), and the simulator was fully restarted for every case to block state accumulation and ensure independence between cases (CARLA_RESTART_EVERY=1, Table 4-5).

Traffic density has three levels — no traffic (none), defensive (def), and aggressive (agg) — and defensive traffic applies courtesy rules that prevent unrealistic behavior (maintaining a minimum gap of 7 m to stopped vehicles, no respawning near evacuation sites) so that evacuation-completion adjudication is not contaminated by NPC spawn artifacts.

For encounter-level safety evaluation, an independent process (hazard_injector) that injects pedestrian dart-out crossings runs in the leaderboard container — a decoupled design that modifies neither the agent nor the runner, so defects in the injection logic do not propagate into the driving stack. Encounter fairness was secured through repeated measurement: (i) spawning starts the crossing not from the sidewalk but from the right edge of the driving lane (+0.5 m), eliminating encounter non-formation caused by spawns outside the guardrail; (ii) 1-second-period re-commanding and walking-speed verification (>1 m/s) block stationary-mannequin encounters; (iii) the trigger uses passage of a fixed point along the route (the dose-response experiment uses a settlement-state trigger); (iv) lead correction matched to ego progress and stopping 12 m after crossing prevent contamination from side contacts and late contacts; and (v) the ego position is obtained from the ROS localization topic (a workaround for the unresolved phenomenon in which the CARLA actor list appears empty from an external client, with the coordinate-frame y-sign flip handled).

The v5 injector adds three things. First, a state-establishment trigger: it subscribes to the supervisor state and the measured speed, and launches the pedestrian at the specified distance ahead, at the right lane edge (lateral jitter ± 0.2 m), only at the moment the state under comparison actually holds — the precondition is verified by the manipulation check so that launching does not depend on the policy behavior. Second, fault-waveform seed fixing (FAULT_SEED). Third, CARLA physics-tick-synchronized recording: ego and pedestrian coordinates, speeds, and separation at every physics frame are recorded to a per-case CSV.

The reliability of the injector itself is managed as part of the experimental infrastructure: survival of the recording channel is guaranteed by a watchdog (runs with lost records are invalid — Section 5), and in the 8 m encounter comparison an arming scheme activates the trigger only after the state under comparison has been confirmed, preventing contamination by state-mismatched encounters.

This section formally reports an adjudication-reliability incident that occurred during the experiments and its reconstruction. The initial implementation adjudicated collisions with a collision sensor attached to the pedestrian. However, it was confirmed by measurement that this sensor never fired in CARLA — it remained silent even in cases where the official adjudicator confirmed a collision. On top of this, the death of the injector's ROS listener caused the loss of separation records, so many cases in the non-intervention arm were misjudged as "avoided" without evidence. This misjudgment was uncovered by visual review of the experiment videos, and the affected data were discarded in full and re-run.

The reconstructed adjudication system has two layers. First, the primary adjudication (primary ground truth) is the real-time ledger of the ego vehicle's collision sensor. The callback of the sensor.other.collision that the official leaderboard adjudicator (CollisionTest) attaches to the ego is patched so that, the moment a collision occurs, it is written to a file together with the counterpart actor identifier (the RAW-HIT ledger). Unlike the official infraction tally, it persists regardless of a case's early or forced termination, and grazes of endpoint structures (static.pole) are classified separately. Second, consistency audits comprise the pedestrian physics oracle and the separation stream. In a vehicle-pedestrian collision, the pedestrian is flung 12–28 m, a kinematic anomaly (speed >4.5 m/s or a jump exceeding 5 m within 1 second), which serves as a cross-check by a computation path independent of the ledger (though not fully independent, since it is the same physics engine). We note the history that the initial 2 m jump threshold falsely flagged normal walking speed (about 3 m/s) and was raised.

In addition, we specify the adjudication pitfalls of the experiment runner's termination labels. (i) The collision label may include contact with endpoint structures — it must be distinguished by the counterpart actor in the ledger. (ii) The hazardous-stop label may include post-collision stops — "no collision" cannot be claimed from the label alone. (iii) The simulator's official infractions are saved only on natural termination — a recording gap in an early-terminated case is not evidence of no collision. All encounter-level safety figures in this thesis are ledger-based.

The clock for latency figures is unified to simulation time. When a hardware-death fault is injected, actor destruction causes a processing stall in the simulator (about 1.6 s) during which simulation time stops; since the world (including pedestrians and traffic) stops with it, the correct clock for safety-related latency is simulation time, and wall-clock measurement overestimates latency by including this stall. The adjudicated latency is computed by recording the injection time (injector) and the state-transition time (supervisor) in simulation time to append-only ledgers independent of case termination, and a stop-before-destroy stream halt ensures that residual frames after destruction do not distort the silence onset time.
6. Distance Ladder and 8 m Encounter Experiment Design

To measure the avoidance/collision boundary by speed, the pedestrian spawn distance was varied as a ladder. (i) Fault-free ladder: fault-free stock stack, spawn distances {14, 11, 8, 6, 5} m × n=4 per distance at a waypoint during normal driving (4.2 m/s). (ii) Blinded ladder: stock under complete LiDAR degradation (lso-high), same distance set (per-distance n as reported in Table 5-3). (iii) 8 m encounter comparison: comparison of the proposed low-speed MRM and stock against an 8 m dart-out under a gn-mid fault (only the EKF localization input contaminated, perception intact) — cf was excluded because traffic-signal reading is impossible and encounters do not form, and gn-high was excluded because most cases end in comfortable stops (the selection process itself corroborates the behavioral differences across faults). (iv) Low-speed ladder: {8, 7, 6, 5} m at the proposed system's nominal 3.0 m/s low-speed cruise (restart cruise; the explicit cap was later found undelivered in these runs — Chapter 5, Sections 7-8). Since the fault-free ladder and the low-speed ladder use different launch protocols, the comparison axis is the encounter speed of "encounters during constant-speed cruising" (specified in Chapter 5, Section 7). (v) Dose-response experiment: after fixing the cap-delivery defect, caps {4.2, 3.6, 3.0} m/s × spawn distances {6, 7, 8, 9} m × 10 seeds (seeds S12–S21, ten in total, with fault waveform, walking speed, lateral jitter, and pedestrian randomness fixed per seed (Table 4-5); gn-mid, injection fixed at 25 s) = 120 runs. Launch uses a settlement trigger rather than a time trigger — the pedestrian is spawned D m ahead at the moment the supervisor is in MRM_MOVE and the measured speed has stayed within the cap-specific band for 1.0 s continuously (bands in Table 4-5) — so that "an encounter under an actually holding cap" is guaranteed at the trigger level. The three cap arms differ only in the value passed through the identical software path (the external velocity-limit interface) (Chapter 5, Section 6). Adjudication follows the ledger standard of Section 5; the exception for runs predating the ledger is stated in Chapter 5, Section 3.

The primary metric of encounter-level safety is the collision rate, reported up front with Wilson 95% confidence intervals. Inferential testing is pre-specified as the single primary endpoint of the dose-response experiment (Chapter 5, Section 6) — the paired 4.2↔3.0 m/s collision difference at the 8 m spawn (exact McNemar) — with the remaining distance-cap combinations reported only as boundary characterization (in small samples, the p-value of exact McNemar changes discretely: even when discordant pairs occur in only one direction, 5:0 gives p=0.0625, not significant, and 6:0 first falls below 0.05 with p=0.03125). Fisher's exact test is used for unpaired auxiliary comparisons. For the dose-response experiment (Chapter 5, Section 6), a single primary endpoint — the paired collision difference between 4.2 and 3.0 m/s at the 8 m spawn (exact McNemar) — was pre-specified before data collection; the remaining distance-cap combinations are reported only as boundary characterization (descriptive statistics with Wilson CIs). As a precondition check on encounter validity (manipulation check), a run with no launch within 420 s, a first-tick encounter speed outside the band (0.15 m/s tolerance), or a spawn violating the ahead-of-ego geometry is rejected and re-run under identical conditions regardless of its outcome. As the exposure metric, distance traveled in the faulted state, deg_dist (distance moved from fault injection to reaching MRC), is defined. The stop-versus-evacuation trade-off is presented along the two axes of collision rate and lane clearance.

1. Main Campaign: Detection Performance and Per-Fault Monitoring and Evacuation Behavior

We begin with detection performance (the premise of RQ1). Table 5-1 summarizes the detection rate and median detection latency for each fault type × severity condition of the main campaign. The proposed detectors achieved detection rates of 96–100% in 11 of the 12 fault conditions — median detection latencies of about 1.0 s for hard fails (cf/lf, ledger re-measurement, simulation time) and 2.1–5.0 s for degradation faults (wall clock — different clock domains, not directly compared), with zero false activations across the 45 fault-free (nf) control cases. The sole exception, mid-severity LiDAR sparsification (lso-mid, detection rate 0.02), falls by design within the tolerated (normal) band above the threshold — even after point dropout at this level, an effective detection range of roughly 55 m remains, the health score does not reach the intervention condition, and the supervisor chooses deliberate non-intervention (continued driving) (Table 5-2). With the present data, however, "tolerance as designed" cannot be separated from "insensitivity of the quality channel," so the detection rate of Table 5-1 should be read as an indicator of intervention eligibility rather than of fault-existence detection. We do not, however, describe this non-intervention purely as a "precise judgment": it overlaps with a detection limitation — the valid-point-ratio channel is insensitive to sparsification at this level — and separating the tolerance judgment from the detection limitation is explicitly stated as future work. The four navigation faults not included in the main campaign (gb correlated bias, gf outage, imb gyro bias, imd bias ramp) were evaluated in a navigation-extension matrix with the same matrix structure (45 cases per condition and method, identical seed pairing): the detection rate was 100% in every condition across the 611/630 valid cases (Table 5-1, bottom, †), and every case converged to localization-confidence-based deferral, exhibiting the same design manifestation as gn-high. We note three observations. (i) The detection latency of imd is inversely related to the ramp slope (median 8.6 s vs. 5.4 s) — an empirical extension of the formulation that small faults are caught later but also become dangerous later. (ii) The detection latency of gf is bimodal: outages while driving are caught at a median of about 3 s, whereas outages coinciding with a stop at a red light are caught only after restarting (21–40 s). This is an intended delay produced by the speed condition of the silence-decay mechanism, which does not treat loss of localization while stationary as an immediate hazard; since the vehicle is stopped, it is not a risk exposure — however, reporting the median alone for a bimodal distribution would be misleading, so we report the two modes separately. (iii) The manner of the deferral stop split along fault type: the GNSS family produced comfortable stops, whereas the IMU family produced hard stops in every case — since even a comfortable stop is trajectory following, the execution layer demotes it to a hard stop when the rotational sense is corrupted.

The graded response in which severity determines behavior was most pronounced in the navigation family. Mid-severity GNSS position noise (gn-mid) accounted for the bulk of shoulder evacuations with 40 of 45 cases, whereas high severity (gn-high) converged to a comfort stop (deferral) in 42 of 45 cases — a manifestation of the design that abandons movement when localization confidence falls below the minimum required for motion. Conversely, under mid-severity LiDAR sparsification (lso-mid), the supervisor chose to continue driving without intervention because the health score did not enter the hazard band (degraded-state driving distance 255 m) — "response proportional to degree," not "stop at every anomaly." As an honest caveat, the main-matrix cases contain no pedestrian dart-out injections, and the case-level "zero collisions" claim rests on data predating the ledger introduced in Chapter 4, Section 5, so we do not use it as evidence for a safety claim (Chapter 6, Section 6).

The primary utility of monitoring is shortening the exposure of driving in a degraded state. In the non-intervention (mrm-off) observations (one run per fault type), the stock stack effectively completed the route without detecting the injected fault: degraded-state driving distances were 238 m for camera death, 240 m for camera noise, 251 m for GNSS position noise, 264 m for LiDAR sparsification, and 275 m for LiDAR clutter (only under IMU noise did the stack stop on its own, at 71 m). Excluding lso-mid, the deliberate non-intervention case, the degraded-state driving distance in the camera and navigation families was 32–58 m for the proposed method (detection + evacuation) and 9–18 m for detection + in-lane stop; for LiDAR clutter and IMU noise it was 11–12 m and 8–9 m, respectively. In short, without monitoring the exposure is "the entire route," whereas with monitoring the exposure becomes a choice variable of the response strategy — the in-lane stop minimizes exposure at the cost of leaving lane occupancy behind, while evacuation accepts tens of meters of controlled exposure in exchange for the possibility of lane clearance and reaching a safe position. The safety-side cost of this trade-off is quantified by the encounter experiments in Sections 4–6.
3. Distance Ladder: Measuring the Avoidance/Collision Boundary

With the fault-free stock stack driving at 4.2 m/s, the results by pedestrian dart-out spawn distance showed a clear staircase: at 14 m and 11 m, all 4/4 per distance were avoided (of each 4, 2 are post-ledger runs adjudicated by the ledger and physics oracle, and the other 2 are pre-ledger runs adjudicated by the runner and video), while at 8, 6, and 5 m all 4/4 at each distance collided (Table 5-3, Figure 5-3). The avoidance/collision boundary thus lies in the 8–11 m interval. This agrees with the stopping-distance model d = vτ + v²/2a (τ≈1.5 s, a≈3.5 m/s²), which predicts d(4.2)=8.8 m, and establishes two things: (i) the choice of 8 m as the dart-out distance in subsequent experiments is a grounded choice of "just below the boundary where avoidance becomes physically impossible," and (ii) the speed→boundary design approximation is self-consistent in the near-boundary regime (same data as its calibration source — not an independent validation; Chapter 3, Section 6), so the effect of the speed cap can be interpreted within the same approximation.

4. The 8 m Encounter: Low-Speed MRM versus Stock

We now present the comparison for a pedestrian dart-out 8 m ahead under the GNSS position noise (gn-mid) fault state. Since gn is a navigation fault that corrupts the EKF localization input while the perception sensors (LiDAR, camera) remain intact, all three conditions share the same pedestrian-detection capability, and only the effects of speed and policy are compared. The stock stack (holding 4.2 m/s) collided in all 10 runs (0/10 avoided). In contrast, the condition in which the proposed system was in low-speed settled cruise (measured encounter speed about 3.0 m/s; Section 6) avoided the pedestrian in all 8 runs and subsequently completed shoulder evacuation (8/8; auxiliary Fisher's exact test p=2.3×10⁻⁵). Because 8 m is shorter than the required stopping distance at 4.2 m/s (8.8 m) — an unavoidable region — but longer than that at 3.0 m/s (5.79 m) — an avoidable region — not outside the required stopping distance at 3.0 m/s (5.79 m), this outcome is exactly what the physics model of Section 3 predicts. The important finding is the third condition: even the same proposed system collided in both of its runs during the transient immediately after fault detection, while deceleration was still in progress (speed at encounter 3.5–3.8 m/s). That is, the protection of the low-speed MRM is effective only after deceleration completes, and residual risk concentrates in the post-detection transient from detection to reaching the settled speed. This transient observation is the starting point of the discussion in Chapter 6, Section 2.
5. Low-Speed Ladder: Shift of the Boundary

In low-speed settled cruise (nominal 3.0 m/s cap configured), the boundary was measured empirically by lowering the spawn distance (Table 5-4). At 8 m the outcome was 8/8 avoidance (Section 4), while at 7, 6, and 5 m the vehicle collided in 2/2 runs at each distance, so the avoidance/collision boundary at 3.0 m/s lies in the 7–8 m interval. Compared with the 8–11 m boundary at 4.2 m/s, the measurements confirm that the reduction of encounter speed moved the boundary inward. Three points are stated explicitly, however. First, the low speed of this ladder stems from the restart profile rather than the explicit cap (Section 6), and the comparison axis is the measured encounter speed. Second, the launch protocols differ — the 4.2 ladder launches into the path of normal driving, whereas the 3.0 ladder launches during restart cruise, and the axis of comparison is the encounter speed of an "encounter during constant-speed cruise." Third, the measured boundary (7–8 m) lies farther out than the pure prediction of the physics model (5.79 m). The difference is explained by the margin required against a moving target and by the off-nominal segment of the acceleration profile immediately after restart, and the model should be interpreted as a lower-bound approximation. Taken together, the per-speed boundaries are 4.2 m/s → 8–11 m and 3.0 m/s → 7–8 m: low-speed encounters physically narrow the range of "unavoidable dart-outs," and its effect and its limit (the transient) are consistently explained by stopping-distance physics.

6. Causal Verification of the Speed Cap: A Dose-Response Experiment on Settled Encounters

The two ladders of Sections 3 and 5 used different launch protocols, limiting direct cross-speed comparison. A controlled dose-response experiment was therefore performed, on the corrected implementation, exclusively on settled-state encounters in which the cap actually held.

The design is a paired matrix of caps {4.2, 3.6, 3.0} m/s × spawn distances {6, 7, 8, 9} m × 10 seeds = 120 runs (Chapter 4, Section 6 (v)). The 4.2 m/s arm is a high-cap control practically equivalent to the road speed limit (15 km/h ≈ 4.17 m/s), and the three arms use the identical external velocity-limit interface differing only in the value, so there is no software-path difference. Launch uses the settlement trigger — the pedestrian is spawned D m ahead at the moment the supervisor is in MRM_MOVE and the measured speed has stayed within the cap-specific band for 1.0 s continuously (spread ≤ 0.25 m/s) — which, unlike time-based launching, guarantees at the trigger level that the cap holds at the encounter. The primary endpoint (8 m, paired 4.2 vs 3.0 exact McNemar) and the manipulation-check adoption rule were pre-specified in a plan before data collection (Chapter 4, Section 7). The 120 runs passing the manipulation check are analyzed (5 failing runs were rejected before their outcomes were examined and replaced by identical-condition re-runs); adjudication is based on the ego ledger (RAW-HIT).

7. Hard-Fail Decision Latency: Verifying the 1.5 s Deadline

For the detection and decision of hard fails (signal loss), a 1.5 s deadline is set as the design specification (an internal requirement) — not a claim of FTTI compliance for a specific safety goal (Chapter 3, Section 4). The latency budget consists of the freshness deadline of 0.85 s and roughly 0.15 s for score propagation and state transition (the fast decision path of Chapter 3, Section 5: skipping persistence confirmation once death is confirmed, skipping grace and retry for unrecoverable conditions, pre-computing candidate paths), for a budget total of about 1.0 s, leaving margin against the deadline. Compliance was verified in ledger-based simulation time over the full cf and lf matrices (90 executed cases each, same structure as the main campaign; the latency n counts runs with parsable ledger latencies and the MRM denominators count runs judgeable after the ledger introduction, both below 90 after simulator-failure exclusion) (Table 5-6, Figure 5-1): across all subtypes the median was about 1.0 s and the maximum 1.20 s with no violations, and MRM attainment was maintained in full. This deadline is limited to hard fails — the decision for degradation-type faults is inherently a matter of statistical evidence accumulation and thus follows the severity-proportional principle (Chapter 3, Section 4).

1. The Temporal Trade-off Between Stopping and Evacuation

The structure running through the entire experiment is the temporal trade-off between stop-type and evacuation-type MRMs. In this sample, the in-lane stop showed the lowest collision rate even under the worst-case condition of transient-window launches (Chapter 5, Section 5), but its price is sustained lane occupancy (Chapter 5, Section 2); evacuation accepts controlled moving exposure and residual transient risk, but on success clears the lane and moves to an off-lane refuge position. Lane clearance is an indicator of relinquishing lane occupancy, not proof that the final position is safer — secondary risks at the shoulder (e.g., approaching rear traffic) were not directly compared in this study. Neither is unconditionally superior, and the choice should follow the temporal structure of the fault (hazard grace, remaining capability, and time to complete deceleration) — a result that supplies concrete selection variables to the ISO 23793-1 framework, which calls for principles of MRM type selection.
2. The Post-Detection Transient, the Overall Fault-Response Risk Window, and FTTI

The fact that all collisions in the evacuation arm occurred in the segment where deceleration was not yet complete, with none during settled cruise (Chapter 5, Section 4: transient 2/2 collisions vs. settled 0/8; Chapter 5, Section 6: all settled encounters avoided), signifies the temporal localization of residual risk — even under the same policy, "when the encounter occurs" dominates the outcome. To distinguish the timeline terms: the post-detection transient runs from the detection instant (t_detect) to reaching the settled speed, whereas the overall fault-response risk window runs from fault onset to reaching the settled speed (T_detect + T_deceleration), the interval governed by Eq. (3-7). The present results concretize this general point into a measurable proposition: "earlier detection (shortening T_detect) and faster deceleration (shortening T_deceleration — in tension with ride comfort and rear-end risk) are experimentally supported as means of shrinking the overall fault-response risk window" — however, since this is an observational comparison rather than a causal experiment in which the detection instant was independently manipulated, it must not be read as an estimate of causal effect size.
3. The Role of the Speed Cap: Causal Effect and Limits

The dose-response experiment on settled encounters in which the cap actually holds (Chapter 5, Section 6) detected the causal effect of the cap: paired discordance 10:0 at 8 m (p=0.002) and a monotone inward shift of the boundary (beyond 9 m to about 7 m). The cap's role is thus twofold — in the settled regime it verifiably moves the avoidance boundary inward, while in the transient it does not yet hold (encounter speeds 3.5–3.8 m/s measured in the Section 4 transient runs). That is, the cap's value is an explicit re-acceleration-suppressing upper bound that does not depend on natural deceleration, but its protection is effective only after deceleration completes. The 3.0 m/s value is grounded but not claimed optimal (the 9 m boundary of the 3.6 arm only locates an intermediate dose), nor is it a formal closed-loop speed guarantee; the verification is further restricted to the gn-mid single fault on a single evacuation corridor (Chapter 5, Section 6).

The lesson of the collision-sensor silence incident (Chapter 4, Section 5) is a general one. In simulation-based safety evaluation, "zero collisions" is meaningful only after the adjudication channel has been proven alive; this study addressed this through positive-control verification of the adjudication sensor, cross-checking against the physics oracle, and explicit statement of the pitfalls of termination labels and official infractions. The undelivered speed cap (Chapter 3, Section 6) carries the same lesson — a publish record is not evidence of delivery, and actuation commands must be verified by their downstream effect (measured vehicle speed). In particular, the error of reading "absence of a record" as "absence of an event" arises structurally in automated large-scale experiments, and the real-time ledger was the effective remedy. The availability of the adjudication infrastructure itself belongs to the same lesson — a watchdog was placed on the recording channel, and data from intervals in which channel liveness was not confirmed were not used for adjudication (watch the watchers).
5. The Cost of Design Conservatism and the Execution and Map Layers

One of the factors limiting the evacuation completion rate (Chapter 5, Section 1) is the cost of intended conservatism. The traffic-light observability gate ("do not send a vehicle that cannot read signals to candidates routed through signalized intersections") shrinks the candidate set under camera-family faults and limits the evacuation completion rate (cf 16/45) — since mitigations (detour search, relaxed V2X trust) would introduce new trust assumptions, the conservative default was retained. The dependence on the execution layer is also stated explicitly: the shoulder-entry maneuver is delegated to the stock goal_planner, so evacuation-incomplete cases mix the decision layer's choice to defer with the execution layer's failure to complete the maneuver (in cf, 27 deferrals vs. 2 incompletions during the maneuver). Deferral is not a system failure but an intended policy choice of the supervisor, and the decision layer's deferral and the execution layer's maneuver incompletion are distinguished at the log level (Chapter 3, Section 8). At the map layer, manual annotation limits the scope of verification, and the traffic-light miscount (Chapter 4, Section 3) showed that map annotation quality is a hidden confounding variable — the fundamental remedy is automated extraction and verification of HD map attributes.

The numerical results of this study are limited to the following scope. (i) This is a case study with a single map (Town07), a single speed limit (15 km/h), and two pedestrian launch corridors. The per-speed boundaries (8–11 m, 7–8 m) and the dose-response results (Chapter 5, Section 6) are values for the low-speed ODD; in high-speed environments the boundaries, the post-detection transient, and the overall fault-response risk window all grow — generalizable claims are restricted to structure (the stopping-distance dependence of the boundary, the concentration of risk in the transient, and the stop/evacuation trade-off), not to the numbers. (ii) Observations about Autoware (non-detection by its own diagnostics, stop-only fallback) are limited to the evaluated 0.39.0 version and this execution configuration, and are not claims about Autoware in general. (iii) The dose-response experiment has n=10 per cell, so the confidence intervals of the boundary characterization are wide and small-sample point estimates can shift with larger samples — this is why collision rates and confidence intervals are reported up front and testing was restricted to the single pre-specified test. (iv) The case-level collision-free status of the campaign matrix (Table 4-3) comes from data predating the introduction of the ledger, and re-verification against the ledger was not performed (the risk is low since these cases have no pedestrian injection, but this is stated explicitly as a gap in methodological consistency). (v) The threshold of the minimum-separation (min-gap) metric recorded as an auxiliary encounter-proximity measure (1.25 m) is a lateral-approach criterion and may be an overestimate for longitudinal approaches. (vi) The gap between the commanded pedestrian speed ({2.5, 3.0} m/s) and the measured speed stems from the walker controller's post-spawn acceleration transient — in the tick-instrumented encounter runs (n=90), the median is 2.46 m/s in the 0.5 s window (1.2–3.0) and 2.50 m/s in the 1 s window, reaching about 95% of the command thereafter. In the encounter experiments, the commanded speed is fixed per seed and measured speeds are logged at physics-tick rate; physical interpretation of the boundary should rest on the measured distribution, not the command. (vii) The phenomenon in which the CARLA actor list appears empty from an external client remains of unknown root cause and is being worked around. (viii) The risk-linked dynamic detection budget (τ_detect) was not directly ablated against a fixed freshness deadline — what this study demonstrates are the effects of continuous health, graded selection, and settled low speed; verifying the increment of the dynamic budget itself is left to future work. (ix) Quantification of the detection latency's margin relative to the hazard time (T_hazard − T_detect), i.e., detection deadline compliance, could not be performed because the hazard event time (T_hazard) cannot be derived within the present measurement structure — this remains future work requiring an instrumentation extension for hazard event timing, and is left together with the explicit FRTI-and-margin reservation deferred as future work in Chapter 3, Section 4. (x) Real-vehicle validation was not performed.

This study proposed a behavior-tree-based monitoring scheme that estimates sensor faults as continuous health scores, together with an MRM supervision layer that selectively chooses between evacuation and stop deferral according to the fault's type, severity, and remaining capability, and that imposes a conservative fixed speed cap (3.0 m/s), back-calculated from stopping distance, on evacuation movement; both were validated in an Autoware-CARLA closed loop. Across the 1,862 valid cases of the experiments, the proposed detectors achieved detection rates of 96–100% in every fault condition except mid-severity LiDAR sparsification, a tolerated band by design — median detection latencies of about 1.0 s for hard fails (cf/lf, ledger re-measurement) and 2.1–5.0 s for degradation faults, with no false activations in the 45 fault-free cases; monitoring shortened faulted-state exposure — a representative unmonitored observation, one run per fault type — from 238–251 m to 32–58 m for the camera and navigation families (LiDAR clutter: 275 m to 11–12 m), and the severity-based evacuation/deferral branching and continued driving under low-risk faults emerged as designed. Safety was quantified through pedestrian-encounter experiments whose adjudication reliability was secured at the methodological level: the avoidance/collision boundary was 8–11 m at 4.2 m/s (model 8.8 m, consistent) and 7–8 m at 3.0 m/s (model 5.79 m — a lower-bound approximation); in fault-state 8 m encounter reproductions, native continuation collided in every run while the proposed low-speed settled cruise avoided in every run (0/10 vs 8/8), and the same policy collided when encountered during the deceleration transient (2/2). A dose-response experiment on settled encounters where the cap actually held (3 caps × 4 distances × 10 seeds = 120 runs, pre-specified) detected the collision-reduction effect of cap 4.2 vs 3.0 m/s with paired discordance 10:0 at 8 m (exact McNemar p=0.002; settled regime, single fault type gn-mid), and the avoid/collide boundary moved inward monotonically as the cap was lowered (beyond 9 m to about 7 m). Hard fails (signal loss) are detected and adjudicated within a 1.5 s design deadline via a fast decision path that distinguishes the nature of the evidence (measured maximum 1.20 s across the full matrix, Chapter 5, Section 7).

The conclusions can be summarized in three sentences. First, shoulder evacuation is not a panacea — stopping and evacuation constitute a temporal trade-off between immediate collision risk and lane clearance / a safe position, and the choice must follow the temporal structure of the fault. Second, the residual risk of evacuation is concentrated in the post-detection transient (from detection until the settled speed is reached), while low speed after settling verifiably moves the avoidance boundary inward (transient encounters 2/2 collided vs settled 0/8; dose-response 10:0, p=0.002) — a transient/settled observational comparison — the experiments support that earlier detection and faster deceleration would shrink the overall fault-response risk window (detection latency + deceleration time) (this is not a causal manipulation experiment), and an encounter-level quantitative observation supporting the need to shorten detection and response times (widening the margin within the FTTI) is presented. Third, simulation-based safety claims hold only on top of a validated adjudication framework — the dual adjudication of the real-time ledger and the physics oracle, together with the explicit identification of recording pitfalls, is the methodological contribution that underpins the figures in this study.

Future work includes extension to high-speed ODDs and multiple maps; introducing survival analysis of lane-clearance time; formalizing the detection budget (explicit reservation of FRTI and margin, and quantification of deadline compliance based on T_hazard measurement); validating the health-score-proportional variable speed cap (implemented, not yet evaluated); designing early-detection and deceleration profiles that reduce the overall fault-response risk window; automatic extraction of HD-map candidates; searching for detour routes without traffic lights; extending the dose-response experiment to multiple faults and corridors; and real-vehicle validation.

Finally, we note a methodological implication. The adjudication framework of this study (real-time ledger, physics oracle) and the encounter-experiment protocol (same-seed pairing, settlement triggers that confirm the state under comparison, pre-specified endpoints, manipulation-check adoption rules) are not tied to any particular system. Follow-up studies that compare MRM and fallback policies in simulation can reuse this protocol regardless of policy implementation; in particular, the principle of "never reading the absence of a record as the absence of an event" and the launch design that prevents the policy from determining whether an encounter occurs remain valid in any comparative experiment.
